figures.caption: Table 1: Cross-session re-identification and MI decoding (%) at the reported operating points. XD = XDAWN+SVM, SPD = SPDNet-ID, CSP-S/L = CSP-SVM/LDA. Worst is over the five attackers. The fixed utility decoder, FBCNet on BCI-IV-2a and EEGNet on OpenBMI, is shown in bold, so every cost is within-decoder. ∆ is defended minus band-limited. Chance is 11.1% and 1.85% for re-identification, 25% and 50% for decoding.

Figure 2: Privacy–utility curves on BCI-IV-2a, varying one strength with the other three at (0.9, 0.35, 0.6, 0.0); the circle marks the selected point. Left: γrma moves both axes together, so under-aligning costs privacy and accuracy at once; the inset expands the flat tail. Right: γscw trades roughly a point of accuracy per point of privacy, and the open marker at 0.80 leaves the frontier. CSP-SVM binds throughout; chance is 11.1% (dotted).

Figure 3: Subject identity and motor-imagery class, measured the same way, Session 2 on BCI-IV2a. Separate colour scales: class differences in band power are far smaller than differences between people, 0.25 against 3.24 undefended. Class deviation is uneven, tongue and left hand being more visible in per-channel power than right hand or feet, which is why decoders use spatial filters. The four subjects shown are the most identifiable of the nine.

Table 2: Stage ablation, cross-session S1→S2, at each reported operating point. Privacy is the worst of five attackers; utility is FBCNet on BCI-IV-2a and EEGNet on OpenBMI. Tied fixes γrma = γscw. Chance 11.1% and 1.85%.

Table 3: Alignment baselines against no defense and the proposed transform, cross-session S1→S2, at each dataset’s reported operating point and under the attacker configuration of Section 5. EA is He & Wu (2020); RPA-RS is recentring and scaling after Rodrigues et al. (2019), without its rotation step (Section 8). Decoder is FBCNet on BCI-IV-2a, EEGNet on OpenBMI. Chance is 11.1% and 1.85%. Every row uses the same attacker configuration, including XDAWN maximised over nfilter ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8}; the RPA-RS rows select nfilter = 8.

Table 7: Sub-band operation, cross-session S1→S2 at each dataset’s reported operating point, under the attacker configuration of Section 5. The full-band row is the reported defense and reproduces Table 1’s CSP cells. Chance is 11.1% and 1.85%.

Table 8: Session-level linkage on BCI-IV-2a at (0.9, 0.35, 0.6, 0.0), rank-1 accuracy (%) over twenty draws. Chance is 11.1%. With nine subjects accuracy is quantised in steps of 11.1 points, so a single subject changing outcome moves a cell by that much; individual defended cells should not be read as differing from one another.

Table 9: Session-level linkage on OpenBMI at (0.9, 0.60, 0.6, 0.2), rank-1 accuracy (%) over twenty draws. Chance is 1.85%. With 54 subjects the quantisation is 1.85 points, so these cells resolve the claim that the BCI-IV-2a table cannot.

Figure 4: Cross-session linkage on OpenBMI, Session 1 (circles) against Session 2 (crosses), coloured by subject, t-SNE from the tangent space at the population Riemannian mean. Undefended, each subject’s sessions form one cluster; defended, they do not. The ratio above each panel is computed in the full 210 dimensions, not the projection, and t-SNE is fitted per panel so distances are not comparable between them.

Table 10: Subject-mean alignment strength γrma, cross-session, with (γscw, α, β) held at (0.35, 0.6, 0.0) on BCI-IV-2a and (0.60, 0.6, 0.2) on OpenBMI. Worst is over SVM, XDAWN, CSPSVM and CSP-LDA. Utility is FBCNet on BCI-IV-2a, EEGNet on OpenBMI. Chance is 11.1% and 1.85%.
Table 11: Whitening strength γscw, cross-session, with (γrma, α, β) held at (0.9, 0.6, 0.0) on BCIIV-2a and (0.9, 0.6, 0.2) on OpenBMI. Columns as in Table 10. Chance is 11.1% and 1.85%.

Table 12: Band-Centre Alignment strength α, cross-session, with (γrma, γscw, β) held at (0.9, 0.35, 0.0) on BCI-IV-2a and (0.9, 0.60, 0.2) on OpenBMI. Worst is over SVM, XDAWN, CSPSVM and CSP-LDA. Utility is FBCNet on BCI-IV-2a, EEGNet on OpenBMI. Chance is 11.1% and 1.85%.
Table 13: Cleanup strength β, cross-session, with (γrma, γscw, α) held at (0.9, 0.35, 0.6) on BCI-IV2a and (0.9, 0.60, 0.6) on OpenBMI. Columns as in Table 12.
Table 14: BCI-IV-2a HO, n=9 subjects. Positive differences denote a reduction in attacker accuracy (privacy rows) or in decoding accuracy (utility rows).

Table 17: Differential privacy on the trace-normalised trial covariance, BCI-IV-2a cross-session, under the adjacency and sensitivity stated above. Attackers use the configuration of Section 5, including XDAWN maximised over nfilter ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8}. Decoders average three seeds; the Ours row is Table 1’s. Chance is 11.1% and 25%.

Figure 5: Magnitude response over the 8–30 Hz MI band at 250 Hz sampling. Blue: the fifth-order Butterworth used by the privacy stages. Green: the Chebyshev II design as specified by the reference FBCSP toolbox (ap=3 dB, as=30 dB, 2 Hz transition allowance, order 9 from cheb2ord). Red dashed: Chebyshev II(5, 60 dB) with the nominal band limits supplied as the stopband. The first two are equivalent across the MI band; only the third removes it.
